```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r setup}
library(mysteryroster)
backends <- attribute_truth_backends()
crowdkit_available <- isTRUE(backends$available[backends$backend == "crowd_kit"])
truthdiscovery_available <- isTRUE(backends$available[backends$backend == "truthdiscovery"])
```

`vignette("truth-fusion-case-study-midwifery")` fit `majority`, `dawid_skene`, and
`truthfinder` on a real 3-source, 1,806-NPI-year cohort and found, among other things,
that `dawid_skene` and `truthfinder` agree on how to resolve `majority`'s ties only 6.6%
of the time, and that `dawid_skene`'s resolutions are 97.6% attributable to simply
trusting NPPES over one disagreeing source. The response to that finding was **not** to
add a fourth truth-discovery algorithm -- it was to ask whether the problem was the
*evidence* going into the existing ones: three source families, two of them (DAC and
PECOS) already known to share lineage, is not much for any method to separate reliable
from unreliable. This vignette is that follow-up, run as an **independent cross-check**
against a second, separately-built analysis of the same underlying real panel, not as a
competing or duplicate build of it.

## What got added, and what didn't

Two real, previously-unused sources, already sitting in the same project's data
infrastructure, were evaluated against a short list of explicit rules -- never count
multiple rows from one source as independent votes; never count two sources as
independent when they share an upstream feed; never treat historical enrollment as proof
of an address in that enrollment year; never treat a dated download as a dated
observation; never propagate a current record backward without checking (see
`docs/midwifery-evidence-ledger-design.md` for the full list, the source-by-source
verdict, and one rule -- never count a hospital affiliation as a practice address --
that was deliberately rescinded partway through, for reasons that document explains):

- **CMS T-MSIS Medicaid enrollment segments** -- dated intervals (`ENRL_START_DT`/
  `ENRL_END_DT`) of state Medicaid program enrollment, independently sourced from
  NPPES/DAC/PECOS/Open Payments. A real, structurally independent, properly-dated
  candidate -- added.
- **Hospital facility affiliations** -- a single current (2026) snapshot of which
  hospital each NPI is affiliated with, tagged by CCN to that hospital's own state. Added
  as direct `practice_state` evidence per an explicit later instruction overriding the
  original hospital-affiliation-is-not-an-address caution (a CCN is a real physical
  facility with a real state) -- but it turned out to add **zero** claims to this
  specific cohort, because this cohort's transitions only touch calendar years 2016-2019
  and 2022-2025, and the facility-affiliation source is dated 2026 only. Not useless in
  general (it matters for a full, longer-range panel); a real year-range mismatch for
  *this* cohort specifically, found by checking rather than assumed.

Everything below is about the one source that did add real evidence: T-MSIS.

## Merging same-lineage sources before fusion, generalized

The original cohort's claims table already merged DAC and PECOS into one combined vote
(`dac_pecos_combined`) by an ad hoc rule: if they agree, one vote; if they disagree, no
vote; if only one is present, use it. `attribute_claims_collapse_lineage()` is that same
rule, generalized to any declared group of same-lineage sources, so a project doesn't
need to hand-roll it again the next time two sources turn out to share an upstream feed:

```{r collapse-lineage}
claims <- data.frame(
  entity_id = c("1", "1", "1", "2", "2", "2"), attribute = "practice_state",
  source_id = c("dac", "pecos", "nppes", "dac", "pecos", "nppes"),
  claimed_value = c("CO", "CO", "CO", "CO", "NM", "NM"), reference_year = 2024
)
collapsed <- attribute_claims_collapse_lineage(
  claims, lineage_groups = list(dac_pecos_combined = c("dac", "pecos"))
)
collapsed
```

Entity `"1"`'s DAC and PECOS rows agree (`"CO"`), so they collapse to one
`dac_pecos_combined` vote rather than two independent ones; entity `"2"`'s disagree
(`"CO"` vs. `"NM"`), so neither counts rather than arbitrarily picking one. T-MSIS shares
no lineage with any of the three original sources (it is a completely separate CMS data
system), so it needs no collapsing -- it is simply added as a fourth, independent
`source_id`.

## A small illustration of the real pattern, before the real numbers

The real cohort's NPIs cannot appear in this package (see "What this vignette does and
does not show" below) -- the illustration here uses placeholder entity IDs and invented
values, sized and shaped to reproduce the *qualitative* pattern the real run found, not
to stand in for it.

```{r illustration-data}
# P01, P02: only nppes + dac_pecos_combined present, disagreeing 1-1 -- a genuine
# majority tie with just 2 sources. T-MSIS casts the only other vote, so whichever
# value it agrees with wins 2-1: resolved, not arbitrarily picked.
# P03, P04: all 3 original sources present, 2-1 decisive already. T-MSIS dissents to
# the minority side, turning the 2-1 decisive vote into a new 2-2 tie.
claims4 <- data.frame(
  entity_id = c("P01","P01","P01", "P02","P02","P02",
                 "P03","P03","P03","P03", "P04","P04","P04","P04"),
  attribute = "practice_state", reference_year = 2024,
  source_id = c("nppes","dac_pecos_combined","tmsis_medicaid_enrollment",
                 "nppes","dac_pecos_combined","tmsis_medicaid_enrollment",
                 "nppes","dac_pecos_combined","open_payments","tmsis_medicaid_enrollment",
                 "nppes","dac_pecos_combined","open_payments","tmsis_medicaid_enrollment"),
  claimed_value = c("CO","NM","CO",  "CO","NM","NM",
                     "CO","CO","NM","NM",  "CO","CO","NM","NM")
)
```

```{r illustration-majority}
maj3 <- attribute_truth_fusion(claims4[claims4$source_id != "tmsis_medicaid_enrollment", ],
                                method = "majority")
maj4 <- attribute_truth_fusion(claims4, method = "majority")
data.frame(sources = c("3 (no T-MSIS)", "4 (+T-MSIS)"),
           abstained = c(sum(maj3$predictions$abstained), sum(maj4$predictions$abstained)))
```

Adding the fourth source here resolves both of the original ties (P01, P02 -- each had
only 2 sources present to begin with, so T-MSIS's vote breaks a real 1-1 split) and
creates two new ones (P03, P04 -- each was already a decisive 2-1 among 3 sources, and
T-MSIS's dissent to the minority side turns it into a 2-2 tie). Net abstention is
unchanged in this small, deliberately balanced illustration (2 of 4 either way), but both
directions are real and present at once -- exactly the mechanism behind the real result
below: a fourth source does not just "add information" in one direction, it can resolve
some disagreements and manufacture others simultaneously.

```{r illustration-ds, eval = crowdkit_available}
ds4 <- suppressWarnings(attribute_truth_fusion(claims4, method = "dawid_skene"))
unique(ds4$source_diagnostics[, c("source_id", "reliability_score")])
```

Four entity-years is too little data for a fit this small to be a trustworthy
illustration of *learned* reliability on its own -- unlike the rest of this vignette,
this specific number has not been independently verified against a real run in the
environment that built it, so it is left for the reader running this vignette to see
rather than asserted here. The real question it stands in for -- does a method that
weighs sources, rather than just counting them, treat `tmsis_medicaid_enrollment`
differently from a method that only counts votes -- is answered properly below, on the
real 3,556-NPI-year cohort, where it was checked directly against the actual output
files before being reported.

## The real finding, on the real 1,806-case cohort

Full detail, every number independently verified (not just quoted from a summary) and
cross-checked against a second, separately-built analysis of the full 2013-2026 panel
run in parallel: `docs/midwifery-evidence-ledger-results.md`. The headline:

- T-MSIS added 1,339 usable claims across the cohort's 3,556 NPI-years (515 of them had
  *zero* non-NPPES evidence before T-MSIS) -- but agreed with NPPES's own claimed state
  only **50.3%** of the time, essentially chance level.
- Under plain `majority`, that disagreement nets out to **more** abstention, not less:
  691/3,556 (19.4%) before T-MSIS, 759/3,556 (21.3%) after. 225 of the original ties
  were genuinely resolved; roughly 293 new ones were created elsewhere -- both
  directions at once, the same mechanism the illustration above demonstrates.
- That net effect is **not uniform across years**, and the asymmetry lines up with two
  specific transitions a *separate*, full-panel analysis of the same underlying data had
  already flagged as unusual: abstention roughly doubles for the 2017-to-2018 transition
  (8.0% to 19.3%) and *decreases* for 2023-to-2024 (23.7% to 18.9%).
- `dawid_skene` and `one_coin_dawid_skene` both learn T-MSIS is the least reliable of
  the four sources (reliability 0.551 and 0.693, lowest in both fits) -- `truthfinder`
  barely distinguishes any of the four, the same contradictory-reliability-ranking
  finding the original 3-source cohort already showed, now extended rather than
  resolved by adding a source.
- Adding T-MSIS nearly **triples** `dawid_skene`/`truthfinder`'s agreement on how to
  resolve a tie (6.6% to 19.1%) and drops `dawid_skene`'s trust-NPPES share by about 18
  points -- a more encouraging signal than the `majority`-only result alone would
  suggest: `majority` counts every vote equally, so a noisy source can only ever create
  or break ties; `dawid_skene` weighs them, and having already learned T-MSIS is the
  least reliable source, moves toward genuine multi-source synthesis instead.

**The cross-check that made this worth doing.** A completely separate analysis, built
independently, ran the opposite experiment on the full 2013-2026, 219,536-entity-year
panel: instead of *adding* T-MSIS to this 1,806-case cohort, it *removed* NPPES entirely
from the full panel and re-measured which year-to-year transitions still looked like
elevated migration. The 2017-to-2018 transition collapsed from a top-ranked transition to
12th of 13 once NPPES was removed; 2023-to-2024 held up as top-tier. Two independent
methods -- one subtracting the most-trusted source from a full panel, one adding a new,
weakly-corroborating source to a frozen sub-cohort -- reached the same conclusion about
which of two migration spikes is substantially NPPES-dependent and which is not. Neither
test alone would be conclusive; agreeing by two different, independently-built routes is
real evidence, not a coincidence of shared methodology.

## What this vignette does and does not show

It shows that expanding the evidence ledger behind a truth-fusion fit does not uniformly
help or hurt: it can resolve real disagreements and manufacture new ones at the same
time, under the same unweighted vote, and a weighted method's response to the same
expansion can look more encouraging *and* less encouraging depending which diagnostic is
asked (more net disagreement under `majority`; less NPPES-dependence and more
cross-method agreement under `dawid_skene`). It shows that an independent cross-check,
built separately and from the opposite direction, is more convincing than either result
alone -- exactly why this was run as a cross-check rather than a second copy of the
other analysis. It does **not** show which source, or which method, is actually correct
for any real NPI -- no independently verified reference location exists for this cohort
(see `docs/validation-protocol.md`), the cohort itself is anchored to NPPES by
construction (`docs/midwifery-ablation-findings.md` section 0), and the illustration above is
invented data sized to show a mechanism, not a result. Real NPI-level data for this
specific cross-check lives outside this package, by design -- only aggregate counts and
percentages are published here or in `docs/midwifery-evidence-ledger-results.md`.
